title: karma: the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita
hook: an old beggar's bowl is snatched from his hands, and he answers with a song that won't even blame karma

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as the road for people who still want things, walked until weariness or faith arrives.
screen: `ACTION FOR THOSE WHO STILL WANT.` · `NOW, THE BEGGAR'S SONG.`

segments.voice: A begging bowl, snatched out of an old man's hands. His staff, taken. His water pot, gone. Someone throws dirt at him; someone spits. Krishna tells this story when Uddhava admits how hard it is to bear the insults of others. The old man was once rich, a brahmin from Avanti, and a miser who never enjoyed his money or gave any of it away. Then, piece by piece, it was gone. Something turned in him. He left home as a wandering beggar, and the people of the town made sport of him. What he says back is a song, and it refuses to blame anyone you'd expect.
screen: `A BOWL SNATCHED AWAY.` → `A MISER WHO LOST EVERYTHING.` → `HE ANSWERS WITH A SONG.`

segments.voice: The song is sometimes called the Bhikshu Gita, the beggar's song. Its center, in paraphrase: these people aren't the cause of my joy and sorrow. Nor are the gods, nor my body, nor the planets, nor my karma, nor time. The mind is the cause. The mind turns the wheel. Look who's on that list. Karma. In a week about action, a man in the Uddhava Gita declines to blame even his own past deeds for what he feels now. He isn't saying karma isn't real. He's saying the place where sorrow gets made is closer than that. Then he takes the list apart, one suspect at a time. If other people are the cause, it's one body knocking against another; what does the self have to do with it? When your own teeth bite your own tongue, who is there to be angry at? If the gods are the cause, what does that have to do with a self that doesn't change? And on down the list. When something stings, the first move is to find who's to blame: them, the traffic, bad luck, even karma. The beggar keeps walking down the list to the one item he can actually work with, his own mind. That's Krishna's answer to Uddhava about bearing hard words. Not pretending they didn't hurt. Looking at where the hurt is being made.
screen: `NOT THEM, NOT THE GODS, NOT KARMA.` · `THE MIND TURNS THE WHEEL.` · `TEETH THAT BITE YOUR OWN TONGUE.` · `START WITH WHAT YOU CAN WORK WITH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small sorrow from this week and walk the beggar's list slowly: was it them, the day, your body, your luck? Give each suspect its moment, then come to the last stop, your own mind, and simply watch what it's doing with that sorrow, without fixing it. If you pray, you can bring that mind, just as it is, to the One you pray to.
Karma. In the beggar's song even karma isn't blamed: the mind is named as the place where joy and sorrow turn.
Your line: karma, the Bhagavata's Uddhava Gita. The wheel turns in the mind, and that's where the work can start. Until tomorrow.

original.note: Sanskrit: a mendicant, one who lives on alms; the old brahmin becomes one, and his song is called the Bhikshu Gita.

what a scholar hears: Bhagavata Purana 11.23, the song of the brahmin of Avanti, where each suspect, people, gods, body, planets, karma, time, is taken apart in turn.

chat.says: In the beggar's song, who does he blame for his sorrow?
options: Not them, the gods, the planets or even karma: he says the mind turns the wheel.
The townspeople who mocked him; he says they caused all of his sorrow.
The gods; he says they turned against him once he'd lost his money.
chat.meaning: The mendicant's song lists people, gods, body, planets, karma and time, and names the mind as the cause of joy and sorrow.

Avanti.meaning: an ancient city-kingdom, the miser's home

Bhikshu Gita.meaning: the beggar's song, in the Uddhava Gita

brahmin.meaning: a member of the traditional priestly class

Uddhava.meaning: Krishna's friend, who finds insults hard to bear

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 11.23.1–41 (Uddhava on how hard insults are to bear; the miserly brahmin of Avanti loses his wealth, becomes a mendicant and is mistreated)
Bhagavata Purana 11.23.42–57 (the mendicant's song: not people, gods, body, planets, karma or time, but the mind is the cause; the tongue bitten by one's own teeth)
Bhagavata Purana 11.23.58–61 (Krishna's closing words on the song)

notes: Confirm verse ranges for 11.23: Uddhava's admission, the brahmin's story, the song (the list of non-causes is commonly cited at 11.23.42), and the tongue-and-teeth image (around 11.23.51).
The list in the song is given as people, gods, body, planets, karma, time; confirm against the Sanskrit (some translations render 'atma' as the self as well). Not given as a count.
The insults (bowl, staff, water pot taken; dirt thrown; spitting) are summarized from 11.23.33–41; confirm.
'Bhikshu Gita' as a name for the song is traditional; stated with 'sometimes called'.
Krishna's closing words are paraphrased as 'whoever takes this song to heart can bear the hard words of others'; confirm.

Editor pass: the teeth-and-tongue image belongs to the 'other people are the cause' step (around 11.23.50), not the body step; the teach now attaches it there, and 'whom do you punch' became 'who is there to be angry at'. Cut the unverified claim that Krishna says whoever takes the song to heart can bear hard words; the teach now says only that the song is his answer to Uddhava's question.
